name: Nature Photos, Time and Impatience
description: Method replication: same task, timing and design as the paper; the photographs are not the paper's stimuli (they are the CC BY natural and urban sets of Berman et al. 2014, PLOS ONE). Does looking at nature make people less impulsive and make time feel longer? Each participant is randomly assigned to natural or built photographs and sees 25 of them for 10 s each, then a delay-discounting task: "Would you rather have $X now or $100 in [delay]?" for 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 6 months, 1 year, 5 years and 25 years, 10 titrating choices per delay (start $50, adjustment $25 then halved each time), with 5 more photographs between delay blocks. The page records one indifference point per delay, the area under the discounting curve, every choice, and the photographs shown. Afterwards: "How quickly has time seemed to pass?" (1 = time flew, 5 = time dragged), an estimate of the minutes elapsed (plus the actual minutes), age and sex. Rebuilt from Berry et al. (2015), PLOS ONE 10(11): e0141030 (n = 43; nature group less impulsive and estimated longer sessions). Differences from the original study: (1) photographs are the 25 most natural of Berman et al.'s 50 nature images and the 25 most urban of their 50 urban images (by their naturalness ratings; one blurred urban image swapped for the next), not the photo sets of the paper; (2) online instead of a quiet lab room without clocks; (3) the short-interval bisection task (null result in the paper) is not included; (4) condition is assigned by simple randomisation, not block randomisation; (5) the 10 practice choices ($10–$100 now vs $100 in 1 week) follow Berry et al. 2014; (6) the indifference point is taken as the immediate amount after the 10th choice.
author: Berry, Repke, Nickerson, Conway, Odum & Jordan

elements.description: natural = photographs of natural scenes (folder “natural”); built = photographs of built scenes (folder “built”). Compare the two groups on the outcomes below (Mann–Whitney tests, as in the paper).

elements.name: photos_viewed
elements.title: Recorded by the page: the photographs shown, in order, with the phase they were shown in: [{ phase: 'before' | 'after_<delay>', file }]. Each is on screen for 10 s.

elements.name: auc
elements.title: Area under the discounting curve (0–1, higher = more self-control), computed by the page from the seven indifference points (Myerson, Green & Warusawitharana 2001; delays in days, normalised by 25 years).

elements.name: dd_choices
elements.title: Recorded by the page: every titrating choice, keyed by delay: { '1 day': [{ trial, immediate, choice: 'now' | 'later', nowOnLeft }], … }. Each delay starts at $50 now vs $100 later; the first adjustment is $25 and each later adjustment is half the previous one; 10 trials per delay; the indifference point is the immediate amount after the 10th choice. Practice trials are not recorded.

config.description: Between-subjects experiment. Each participant is randomly assigned to look at photographs of natural scenes or of built (urban) scenes, 10 s each: 25 photographs before a delay-discounting task and 5 between its delay blocks. The task asks “Would you rather have $X now or $100 in [delay]?” for 7 delays (1 day to 25 years), 10 titrating choices each, giving one indifference point per delay. Afterwards participants judge how fast time passed and estimate how many minutes have gone by. Method replication of Berry, Repke, Nickerson, Conway, Odum & Jordan (2015), PLOS ONE 10(11): e0141030.

paper.title: Making Time for Nature: Visual Exposure to Natural Environments Lengthens Subjective Time Perception and Reduces Impulsivity
